transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-07-15 08:00 PT | Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Samir Bhatt (Redwood SE), Leo Park (Redwood SRE-notes), Jenna Lee (BrightCart ML Platform Lead), Marcus Chen (BrightCart SRE), Priya Singh (BrightCart CTO), Carlos Rivera (BrightCart Product)

[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — walk through last week's 6 hour run, talk tuning knobs for continuous batching, set concurrency targets and steps for a longer stress run.
[00:18] Jenna: Yep, thanks Ava. we saw pretty good median throughput but had tail spikes around the 3 hour mark. Marcus dug in but we'll need help understanding queuing behavior.
[00:30] Samir: right, so we replayed the trace you sent, t-thanks again, and when we enabled continuous batching with default window sizes we saw batching improved token efficiency but we also hit a queue depth threshold which caused a small backlog and then a tail latency jump.
[00:45] Marcus: that matches what we saw - packets piled up then the system got, like, bursty and then some requests time out, which is bad for product.
[00:58] Ava: okay, quick clarification — when you say timeouts are those client-side 5s timeouts or did you see server-side queuing exceed the SLO?
[01:06] Jenna: mostly client-side, but server p95 did creep up to about 1.4s from a baseline of 0.6s while p99 jumped more, it's in the spreadsheet.
[01:20] Samir: note — the profiler showed KV cache cache hits were high but the K V cash (transcription: KV cache) eviction pattern correlated with short-lived prefix changes, so cache churn amplified work per request.
[01:35] Priya: is there a config to slow down the batching window or to prefer latency over throughput? we care about tail for user-facing flows.
[01:43] Samir: yes, there are a few levers — batching window size, max batch size, concurrency cap and queue length limit which enforces backpressure. for this POC we had window=40ms, max_batch=64, concurrency cap=6. that cap let too many inflight groups form during bursts.
[02:02] Ava: got it. what if we lower concurrency to 4 and increase window to 60ms so batches are fuller but we reduce simultaneous in-flight groups?
[02:14] Samir: that should reduce p99 but will increase median token latency a bit; it's a tradeoff. also enabling adaptive backpressure that rejects or queues at the edge when queue length > threshold helps keep SLOs.
[02:27] Jenna: hmm ok, for checkout we need p99 < 2s. median can float a little. can you target a throughput that meets that?
[02:35] Samir: we can target ~800 requests/s with concurrency 4 and window 60ms given your request size distribution — the earlier run peaked at ~1200 req/s when cap was 6 but with p99 violations.
[02:48] Marcus: is that per-region? we test across US-EAST and EU-WEST, both regions saw similar patterns though eu had slightly higher latency.
[02:58] Samir: yes per-region numbers; network jitter and instance placement impacted eu. we recommended pinning to same zone for test or using lower inter-region fanout.
[03:10] Carlos: just checking — are these hosted Redwood or dedicated instances in this POC?
[03:14] Ava: this POC is on Redwood Dedicated reserved nodes in your sandbox account, so we have control over GPU pool sizing and kernel variants.
[03:22] Jenna: good, also security folks asked about logs and audit — we saw s3 export for logs in the doc but can you confirm retention?
[03:29] Ava: yes we shared the SOC2 and logging config in the security packet; retention defaults to 90 days for this pilot, we can extend or point to KMS managed storage.
[03:37] Priya: perfect. back to throughput — can you explain queueing strategy? are you using token-based batching or request-level batching?
[03:44] Samir: request-level batching with token-aware kernel selection; continuous batching groups requests by key prefixes and sequence length heuristics, then a KV cache is checked to skip tokens. we do have a token budget per batch to avoid long-tail hogging.
[03:58] Jenna: ok do you have a recommended concurrency target table? like small/medium/large request sizes?
[04:04] Samir: yes — small (~<512 tokens) target concurrency 8 for max throughput; medium (512-1024) concurrency 4; large (>1024) concurrency 2. that's a starting point and we can tune per workload.
[04:20] Ava: for BrightCart checkout flows you said median is small but some sessions hit medium — so we'll recommend mixing concurrency profiles and autoscale rules.
[04:29] Marcus: autoscale — is it instant or we set a warm-up? we saw cold spikes when new workers came up causing transient p99 blips.
[04:36] Samir: there's a warm-up policy; we recommend a small buffer pool to handle spikes while new nodes join. also steady-state pool plus burst capacity to handle >95th percentile.
[04:46] Jenna: what about queueing at the client vs server? we'd prefer server-side backpressure so clients get explicit 429s instead of long waits.
[04:53] Ava: agree — we can enable queueing policies so the gateway returns 429 once queue depth hits threshold; that keeps tail latencies predictable.
[05:01] Priya: will that break current client retries? our SDK retries automatically; we might need to adjust backoff.
[05:07] Samir: good point — we'll provide recommended retry strategy (exponential backoff + jitter) and a 429 handling doc.
[05:14] Leo: note — we observed one misconfig where max_batch was set higher than GPU memory allowed which led to OOMs in one run; Samir flagged kernel mismatch then fallback caused higher latency.
[05:26] Samir: yeah, fallback to quantized kernel increased token time. in the run we also saw some mislabelled p95 due to transcription of spans in logs, so please ignore that earlier number in the sheet — use the per-token csv we attached.
[05:40] Jenna: ok, walk me through the proposed test plan for the 12hr run.
[05:45] Ava: plan is: 1) set continuous batching window 60ms, max_batch 64, concurrency cap 4; 2) enable server-side queue limit at 500 requests and 429 policy; 3) run 12hr replay of the representative 24h slice you provide at 1x and 2x arrival rates; 4) collect per-token csv, per-request latencies and GPU metrics; 5) share results and decide on next follow-up.
[06:08] Marcus: sounds good — what telemetry do you need from our side?
[06:12] Samir: the request traces with timestamps and sequence lengths, plus any client-side timeout settings. also a mapping of critical routes (checkout, search) so we can prioritize.
[06:20] Jenna: I'll upload traces to the shared folder after this call.
[06:24] Ava: great. any blockers on security or procurement to run the extended test?
[06:28] Priya: procurement is ok for sandbox. security asked for KMS usage — you said that's available?
[06:32] Ava: yes, we can point logs and model keys to your KMS. we'll swap in customer-managed keys for the next run if you want.
[06:41] Carlos: quick question — competitors — are any other vendors providing similar batching? we evaluated OpenAI and SageMaker; their managed endpoints didn't give same low-level batching control.
[06:51] Samir: correct, most managed endpoints abstract batching; Redwood gives the explicit knobs and kernel selection for quantization and batching.
[06:58] Jenna: ok let's finalize dates: you said Samir will share updated config and spreadsheet by tomorrow?
[07:03] Samir: yes I'll upload by 2026-07-16 EOD, and Ava will kick off the 12hr run once traces are uploaded.
[07:11] Ava: closing notes — recap: lower concurrency to 4, window 60ms, enable queue backpressure + 429s, run 12hr stress test, share results next sync. any other items?
[07:22] Priya: no, thanks.
[07:24] Jenna: thanks everyone.
[07:26] Ava: thanks, we'll follow up in the next sync and post action items in the CRM.

References: benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in chat), security packet (link), per-token CSV (to be uploaded).

End of transcript.
